defects.description: Edge 'SageMaker training -> Training data and artifacts' is typed read but its label also says it writes artifacts; the write direction is not modelled.
The retrain workflow deploys a new model to the live endpoint with no evaluation or approval gate (for example a model registry approval status) before the blue/green update.
No IAM roles or least-privilege execution roles are shown for Lambda, Step Functions and SageMaker access to S3 and DynamoDB.
Cognito user authorizer is assumed for the checkout API without saying whether the caller is the end user's browser or a backend checkout service; machine-to-machine auth may fit better.
To spread the real-time endpoint across two AZs it needs at least two instances; the cost of this always-on minimum is not discussed.

reviews.summary: A complete, correctly wired design with API Gateway plus WAF and Cognito, Lambda calling a SageMaker real-time endpoint with timeout and fallback, DynamoDB for scores, and an EventBridge plus Step Functions monthly retrain with blue/green deployment and CloudWatch alarms.

defects.description: The CloudWatch node has no edges, so the design does not show which components send scoring latency, errors or endpoint metrics, and there is no alarm on failed retraining runs.

No caller node and no edge protection for a payment-path API; HTTP API with IAM auth works for a signed backend caller, but the decision to skip WAF and the caller identity are not stated as assumptions.
The pipeline deploys the new model version straight to the endpoint with no stated evaluation or approval step and no blue/green or canary deployment guardrails.
Multi-AZ placement of the endpoint (minimum two instances) is not stated, so availability on the inline checkout path is unspecified.

reviews.summary: A lean, technically correct design (HTTP API, Lambda with fallback, SageMaker real-time endpoint, DynamoDB, EventBridge-triggered SageMaker pipeline), but monitoring is not wired up and deployment safety and AZ placement are thin.

defects.description: I2 (clean URLs such as /menu returning that directory's index page) is claimed to be met by CloudFront alone. With a private S3 REST origin behind OAC, the CloudFront default root object applies only to the root URL, not to subdirectories, so /menu/ would return an error unless a CloudFront Function or similar rewrites to index.html. The design does not include one.
There is no CloudWatch alarm notification target (for example SNS email), so the bakery would not actually be told when error rates rise.
Cache invalidation after content uploads is not mentioned, so updated menu or hours may be served stale until the TTL expires.

reviews.summary: A correct, low-cost serverless static site (Route 53, CloudFront with ACM in us-east-1, private S3 with OAC, IAM-scoped uploads, CloudWatch), let down by a clean-URL claim that CloudFront does not deliver without a rewrite function.

defects.description: The ACM certificate is placed in a generic 'Primary Region' with no statement that it must be requested in us-east-1; a certificate in any other Region cannot be attached to CloudFront, so HTTPS on the custom domain would fail.
No content update path (who uploads pages and with what IAM permissions) is modelled.

The rationale calls CloudFront 'the only practical way' to serve a custom domain over HTTPS from S3; S3 website endpoints do lack HTTPS, but managed alternatives such as Amplify Hosting exist, so the claim is overstated.
Default root object and subdirectory or index handling are not mentioned, and alarms have no notification target.

reviews.summary: A correct minimal static-hosting design (Route 53, CloudFront, ACM, private S3 with OAC, CloudWatch), but it leaves the required us-east-1 certificate Region unspecified and omits the content upload path.

defects.description: I1 says tokens are validated 'at the edge of the API', but validation actually happens inside the tasks (JWKS fetch), and only AZ A tasks have the JWKS edge.
No container image registry (ECR) or image pull path is shown, though I4 refers to pulling images privately.
Tasks read the DB secret, but the design does not say that tasks must re-fetch credentials after rotation (or use a proxy) to avoid connection failures when the password changes.
No container autoscaling policy or alarm notification is described; CloudWatch receives logs only from tasks, not from Aurora or ElastiCache.
Customer managed KMS keys plus two NAT gateways add fixed cost; the CMK choice is justified only by an inferred requirement.

reviews.summary: A sound two-AZ ECS Fargate design with an internet-facing ALB plus WAF, private tasks, one NAT gateway per AZ for payments egress, Multi-AZ Aurora PostgreSQL and ElastiCache, and Secrets Manager rotation; the gaps are minor (ECR, token validation wording, rotation handling in the app).

defects.description: Only a single NAT gateway in Public subnet A serves payments egress. If AZ A fails, tasks in AZ B lose outbound access to the payments API, which violates the requirement to survive the loss of one AZ.

CloudFront with WAF is the intended single public entry point, but the internet-facing ALB origin is not restricted to CloudFront (no secret origin header rule, CloudFront managed prefix list or VPC origin). Clients can bypass WAF by calling the ALB directly.
ALB, Fargate tasks, Aurora and RDS Proxy are each placed only in AZ A subnets in the diagram, which contradicts the stated two-AZ rationale.
I3 (centralized audit trail) is attributed to CloudWatch; no CloudTrail is included.

The rotation relationship between Secrets Manager and Aurora is not shown (only Secrets Manager -> RDS Proxy), and there are no edges from tasks to Secrets Manager for the payments API key or to Cognito for JWKS.
Putting CloudFront in front of a non-cacheable B2B API adds cost and complexity with little benefit unless caching is disabled and a reason is given.

reviews.summary: A broadly correct ECS Fargate, Aurora, ElastiCache and RDS Proxy design with good additions (ECR, RDS Proxy, PITR), but a single NAT gateway breaks AZ-loss survival for payments calls and the ALB can be reached directly, bypassing CloudFront and WAF.

preference.why: Both host the model on SageMaker correctly, but A wires observability end to end, alarms on failed retraining, uses blue/green model updates and protects the payment API with WAF and an authorizer.
Both are correct low-cost CloudFront plus private S3 designs; A pins the certificate to us-east-1 and models the IAM-controlled upload path, though its clean-URL claim needs a CloudFront Function.
A meets the AZ-loss requirement with a NAT gateway per AZ and has a single protected entry point, whereas B's single NAT gateway and bypassable ALB undermine resilience and the WAF protection.
